Coal is the insidious hero of this book of poetry. “Let’s hear it for the coal,” announces the poet. The coal that was “laid down in times / of swamps and ferns and clumsy monsters hauling / their heavy bodies out of the water. A time / before mountains, before the dinosaurs.” The coal that lay fallow underneath the green hills and valleys of Wales until it was summoned by the incipient industrial revolution. The coal that dragged whole families away from their rural occupations: “There’s no more living / off small-scale wool. The new machines can work / at ten times the speed.” The coal that sent the men and boys underground. Into the darkness, into danger. “A man may take / a canary in his cage along with his tools / when he goes to work, and suddenly it sings / the most beautiful song you’ve ever heard in your life / and collapses.”

The women stayed above ground in the settlements that sprang up around the pithead. They scrubbed floors, baked bread, bore children, and they sang too. “After an evening’s practice, / soprano and mezzo have nailed ‘In Tears of Grief’ / and there’s a small crowd at the door: neighbours / and passers-by, drinking in each phrase.”

Caroline Williamson has rigorously pillaged the archives, tracked down recent forebears, and has constructed vivid “scenes from life” based upon known facts. None of it was very long ago. The first person listed in the cast of characters, Esther Owen, was born in 1850.

This is just the plausible backstory the poet has laid down, to ground us, as it were, before she ruthlessly hauls us through the continuing saga of coal’s inexorable trajectory. Williamson writes of an expedition to an Australian mine. “And now an open pit / gapes deep and black at a weirdly dazzling sky.” As she perches high above, she asks, “Where’s everybody gone?” Down below there’s just one bloke sitting in the cab of an air-conditioned machine, that cuts more coal in a day than a thousand men could.

If coal doesn’t need us anymore, do we need coal? Has the pact broken down? The penultimate poem, “Haul / sun” suggests “a shift in thinking”. Solar panels arrive on the back of a truck to bedeck “the roof on the north side / of our weatherboard house, / the men swing into action”.

I appreciated the symmetry the poet achieves by positioning each discrete poem on one page and by the way the last line of each poem is a hook, to keep us turning the page, to find out what comes next. The special gift of poetry is to distil: it’s the perfect vehicle for the cool intelligence that shaped this eloquent confluence of cause and ever-present, looming effect.

Rabbit Poets Series, 128pp, $25

Jennifer Compton is a poet and playwright.
